narrative.overview:
This is a practical printed document that a family keeps to hand — a handbook the federation printed and the unit filled in. It is not trying to be distinctive. It is trying to be legible, familiar, and recognisably the federation's, so that a parent who has never seen this particular software still knows how to read it: every page opens the same way, every action is a button in the place buttons go, and nothing on screen is competing with the thing they came to do.

Structurally the system is two layers that never mix. A vendored theme — Les Scouts' own template-unite, a Bootstrap build carrying the federation's graphical charter — supplies every shape, colour and typeface. On top sits a single small override file, static/css/troopconnect.css, holding only the deviations: a hero band, the public page's enrolment desk, the member homepage's tile board, a first-run wizard, an agenda grid, one table column with a ceiling. The rule that makes this work is that the override file stays small; a rule that merely restates one the theme already makes is a liability, because the theme can move under it and the local copy would win.

The result is deliberately unglamorous and consistently so. Density follows the task rather than the brand: a settings page is a stack of cards, a member list is a striped table, a form is one labelled field per block. The federation shows up in flat charter colour and in bold Muli — and, in four places, at field scale rather than as an accent: the banner's flag silhouette behind a page title, the ground the enrolment desk stands on, which is the four branches drawn as four columns, the desk's answer, which takes the matched branch's own colour as its ground, and the member board's full-bleed paper ground, which lifts the two branch colours the unit's public page already speaks into a wash behind white tiles. There is no troop-level colour, no theme picker, no second accent: the palette is the federation's, and the unit's identity is carried by its name and the logo it uploads.

The member page is the one surface that composes rather than lists. Its board refuses the equal card grid: tiles carry unequal grow weights, the household's one dark tile sits beside a person's white one, and the tool mosaic repeats the same asymmetry for actions. The composition is still the handbook's — same paper, same inks, same serif — but it is laid out for scanning a family rather than for reading a page.
keyCharacteristics: Bootstrap's own primitives, used as intended, restyled only where a task needs it
One typeface (Muli) and one flat charter palette, both inherited, neither configurable
One green-to-blue bar and a serif page head on the member ground as the recurring opener
Thin 1px lines and 0.25rem corners on the product; the member board's 1.25rem tiles trade the border for one soft charter-blue shadow
Paper-filled fields on a paper-coloured page, separated by a border and a blue focus halo
The homepage's desk standing on the four branches' colours, at the one place the page spends them
A member board of unequal tiles: one dark anchor (balance or lead tool), white person tiles, and branch-tinted tool clusters
Two shells: the site (fixed 84px navbar) and the first-run wizard (its own page, same theme)
A contact sheet and its confirmation reuse the board's white tile; a reader's secondary duties are chips under the summary

rules.name: The Federation's Ink Rule
rules.body: The palette belongs to Les Scouts and a troop never configures it. A troop owns its name, its logo, its favicon, its branches and its content — it does not own colour. A "match my logo" or theme-picker feature is a departure from this system, not a refinement of it.

rules.name: The Charter-Only Rule
rules.body: A new state gets a colour from this list or it gets no colour. Charter hues may carry meaning only through an explicit mapping — today that is the agenda's and the member tiles' three activity types (`charter-blue-deep` reunion, `charter-green-deep` day, `charter-plum` weekend) — and never by inventing a hue or reaching for a Bootstrap default that the theme did not override.

rules.name: The Shared Ground Rule
rules.body: The hero band and the desk are two elements of one field. The band's settle ends on `home-ground` and the desk *begins* on it, with no gap between them, and that is what makes the join invisible. Changing one without the other puts a seam across the top of the public page — and it lands at exactly the height where the photograph stops, which is the most visible line the page could have. Both read it from the one `--home-ground` in `:root` because the two elements are siblings and neither owns it.

rules.name: The One Dark Tile Rule
rules.body: A member page spends exactly one dark surface. It carries the household balance when the reader owes money for a child, and otherwise the first action of the featured tool group. It is never a second decorative note: one dark tile is what makes the rest of the board read as paper. When the household is settled or fees are off, the dark note moves to the tools — the page still has one, and the balance tile is simply absent rather than rendered as a zero. A staff reader's new-members alert is the one exception: when it holds the featured group's first slot the alert takes the page's loud note as a warning tint, and the dark gradient is not stacked under it. The page still spends one loud surface, and it is the one that says there is work to do.

rules.name: The Branch-Tint Rule
rules.body: A tool cluster takes a 6–8% tint of one branch colour over white — children 7% Baladins blue, sections and the unit 6% Louveteaux green, account and site none. The tint names the group; it never becomes the label's colour, and it is mixed over white so the tile stays a tile on the gradient ground.

rules.name: The Crimson-Only-For-Overdue Rule
rules.body: Crimson is spent on money and absence, and only when something is overdue or reported: the late note on the dark tile and the absence line on a person tile. The dark tile takes the same warning as a light rose (#ffd1db) because crimson ink fails on it. No other state borrows the colour.

rules.name: The Two-Voice Rule
rules.body: The application speaks Muli and *names* in Source Serif 4. The boundary is display versus everything else — a unit's name, a section heading, a branch's name, a child's or section's name, a date leaf's day, a member count, the household balance, the desk's closing statement are display; a button, a table cell, a help line, a form label are not, however emphatic. A third face is a departure from this system rather than a flourish within it, and the theme's four decorative faces (Housepaint, CaveatBrush, Mali-Bold, Roboto Mono) are still not it: they are costume, and a title is not a costume.

rules.name: The Two-Scale Rule
rules.body: A new block sizes itself from the override scale above and never from an ad-hoc value; a page's structure keeps to the theme's ramp. Adding a step to either without recording it here is how a system stops being one.

rules.name: The Weight-Not-Colour Rule
rules.body: Emphasis is 700, not a hue. Never colour text to make it louder — the palette has no text colours to spend, and every heading already shares the body's ink.

rules.name: The Board-Numeral Rule
rules.body: A number the reader scans for — the household balance, a section's member count, the day on a date leaf — is set in the display serif with tabular figures. A number inside a sentence stays Muli. The face is the signal that the number is a fact, not prose.

rules.name: The Reader's Register Rule
rules.body: French addresses a plain parent with *vous* and every other reader with *tu* — an animé, a section leader, the unit team. The register follows the board the reader answers for, not their primary role alone: a staff account whose role is Parent still reads the unit's board and is addressed as staff. English and Dutch carry one wording; only the French catalog holds the second key (`informal`).

rules.name: The Asymmetric Board Rule
rules.body: The member board is a flex row with deliberately unequal grow weights, never an equal-width grid: the balance tile is the widest, the first person tile next, the second narrower again, so a row of two reads about 7/5 and a row of three about 45/32/23. The weights wrap; below 768px every tile takes the row. A fixed grid is a hole whenever a family has an odd number of children. The one exception is a family with more than one child: siblings are peers, so the balance stands alone on the first row and the children share equal columns under it — an equal group, not an equal page.

rules.name: The Page-Is-The-Menu Rule
rules.body: A signed-in reader's tools live on the member page, gated one by one on the same predicate their view enforces; the header carries no menu for them. A link kept in two places is two things to keep honest, and a link whose gate has moved is a dead end. The page is the menu. The one exception is the way back: a member page names the board above its title, because the rule only holds for a reader who can reach the page the menu is on.

rules.name: The Border-or-Shadow Rule
rules.body: Never both on the same surface. If a card needs a shadow, its border goes; if it needs a border, it gets no shadow. The two are the same signal, and using them together makes a surface look like two. On the member board the trade is explicit: the tiles have no border at all, because a 1px line on the gradient ground reads as a seam.

rules.name: The Flat-Page Rule
rules.body: The page itself is flat. No section, band or container lifts off the background — depth is spent only on cards that behave as separate units, and never as decoration. The member board's tiles are those units at page scale; the ground between them is still one flat light.

rules.name: The One-Entrance Rule
rules.body: One surface gets an authored entrance, and it is the one the visitor operates. Everything else acknowledges a state change and stops. A page of staggered section reveals is not this system.

rules.name: The Finish-Without-It Rule
rules.body: Every keyframe states only where the thing comes *from*; the resting state is always the element's own rule, never the animation's end frame. An animation that never runs — a browser without them, or a reader who has asked for less motion — therefore delivers the finished design rather than half of it. Nothing is ever hidden waiting for script.

rules.name: The Reduced-Motion Rule
rules.body: `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` removes the distance and keeps the arrival. The rail is simply already drawn, and the band appears as one object, colour and sheet together, in a 200ms fade — the state change still registers, and nothing moves. The chip and the segment a parent touched were already confirmed in their own colour by then, so no choice is ever answered with silence.

rules.name: The Never-On-The-Field Rule
rules.body: Copy is never set *on* a charter field. White type fails AA on the Baladins blue and dark type fails on the other three, so the paper goes between them every time. The field may carry meaning; it may not carry words.

rules.name: The Ink-Not-The-Colour Rule
rules.body: A branch's colour is stated twice on the page and written once. The room, the rule and the mark take the colour at the strength their ground allows; the branch's *name* — in the rail, on the chosen year, in the sentence that names it — takes `BRANCH_INKS`, which is the same hue darkened until it can be read. These are not two colours. They are one colour used for two jobs that do not have the same requirement, and no branch is ever renamed by it: Baladins' room is still #00a0de.

dos: Do load the vendored theme first and `troopconnect.css` second — the order is what makes the override layer work, and reversing it silently disables every deviation.
Do keep `troopconnect.css` small. Only put a rule there that the theme does not already state; a restated rule is a copy that can win after a theme upgrade.
Do pair a `.btn-primary` with `.btn-outline-primary` on the same row, and give a destructive action an outline button — Deregister, Remove and Detach are all outline, never filled.
Do give every field a `<label class="form-label" for="...">`, then the control, then `.form-text` for help — in that order.
Do use `role="alert"` on errors and `role="status"` on confirmations, and keep errors as text under the control rather than as a red field.
Do wrap every `.table` in `.table-responsive`, and put a `max-width` on a free-text cell instead of letting the row grow.
Do open every members page with the page head (`hat_title` + `hat_text`): the title in the display serif on the member ground, never a coloured band.
Do ship a plain `href` or `action` alongside every HTMX attribute, so the page still works when the swap does not.
Do set the navbar's 84px height in px and keep `--site-navbar-height` in px to match; the navbar does not scale with the root font size.
Do state the household balance once, above the person tiles, and never per child — the household is the billing unit, and the eldest child pays in full.

Do build the member board as a flex row with unequal grow weights, so one, two or four tiles each fill their row without the equal-card symmetry — except a multi-child family's children, which are equal peers under the balance tile.
Do spend exactly one dark tile per member page: the balance when there is money owed, otherwise the featured group's first action.
Do give each person tile a date leaf, a type chip and an absence state when the agenda is on; when it is off, remove the whole block rather than leaving an empty leaf.
Do mix tool-cluster tints at 6–8% over white, and keep the label in the page ink rather than in the tint.
Do set board numerals in the display serif with tabular figures, and keep numbers inside sentences in Muli.
Do address a plain parent with *vous* and every other French reader with *tu*; the register follows the board the reader answers for, not the primary role field alone.
Do keep a field's paper fill when it takes focus, and keep the success toast's words in the ink: white on the bright green is 2.1:1.
Do use the solid ink focus outline on a whole-tile link, and white on the dark tile.
donts: Don't edit anything under `app/static/vendor/template-unite/`. It is byte-identical to a known upstream commit, and a local edit is lost at the next theme refresh and invisible in the diff that would have caught it.
Don't introduce a colour. The palette is the federation's — if a new state needs a colour it takes one from the list above or it takes none.
Don't set Housepaint, CaveatBrush, Mali or Roboto Mono. The application speaks Muli; those faces exist in the theme for pages this project does not build.
Don't put a border and a shadow on the same card — that is two signals for one surface.
Don't colour body or heading text to add emphasis. Weight is the tool.
Don't style the site header with a bare `header` selector. The public page's hero band is a `<header>` too, and a bare selector reaches into it.
Don't use `window.alert()` for feedback. Toasts and inline alerts exist, and a browser alert cannot be translated or styled.
Don't build a second modal. `#modal` / `#dialog` is the dialog, and every HTMX view targets it.
Don't paint a form control white on a white sheet, and don't let the theme's final form rule do it: the paper well is the field's identity.
Don't let a successful modal close in silence. The dialog closes onto the non-autohiding toast; a confirmation page carries the promise.
Don't give a parent's absence line a door; only the section leader's line has somewhere to go.
Don't add a page that has to be read on hover to be understood — nothing in this system depends on pointer state to be legible.

Don't put a mask or a clip on a container whose children are meant to paint outside it. Both clip to the element's own border box, so a fade that lives one level too deep cuts off exactly the overflow it was placed to soften — the desk field's mask sits on the field's full-width box, never on the container its bleeds are supposed to cross.

Don't put a balance or a Pay button on a child's tile. Fees are per household and the finance views 404 for anyone without access; the treasurer sentence — and the message door when a treasurer is named — is the honest version for a parent.

Don't replace the member board with an equal-width card grid. The unequal grow weights are the composition, and a fixed grid leaves a hole on an odd number of children. Equal columns belong only to siblings under a balance tile, never to the board as a whole.
Don't add a header menu for signed-in readers. The page is the menu, and a link kept in two places is two things to keep honest.
Don't use a branch's full-strength colour as a tile ground. Tints stay at 6–13% over white, and the one dark tile is a darkened mix of two branch colours, not a charter field.
Don't let a long name or activity title truncate inside a tile. Names run to 150 characters and titles to 200; they wrap with `overflow-wrap: anywhere` and a `min-width: 0` on the flex/grid child.
Don't give the member page a second dark surface or a second primary action. One dark note, one lead tile, and the rest of the board is paper.
